scenario: AITA for refusing to loan my brother my vacation money? | My (21F) brother (30M) and I live with our parents. He’s in a shitty job trying to get out so he went back to school and that’s why he moved back in 1 1/2 years ago. I’m in third year university and working to put myself through. I’m in business school which I am finding to difficult but not impossible. I should graduate in 2 years. When I got into uni I started saving for a bit of all my paycheques (whatever I could manage; sometimes it was as much as 15% and others as low as 1%) to go on a big vacation post uni gradation. Probably a cruise, Japan or a trip to different countries in Europe I’ve never been to. It has about $2800 in it now. My brother has not been on a vacation in many years and keeps hinting that he needs one. My parents already help him financially so he wouldn’t ask them for more help for that. Last week when he was complaining to my parents about it, they mentioned me and my vacation fund and said he could’ve been doing that all these years to be able to afford to go somewhere, or he could start now and maybe be able to go across country in a year. 3 days ago he came to me and asked if he could borrow my vacation money to go on a trip to Japan this summer or Fall. He said since I won’t need it for another 2 years it’s plenty of time for him to pay me back. I said no. My brother is horrible with money. He makes about as much as I do yet always seems to be broke despite never buying groceries or paying rent (for the record, I do not pay rent either, which is why I have been able to build up the fund, but I do buy most of my own groceries, as well as pay for all my makeup, health supplies, phone and uni fees). He’s very mad I said no. He says it’s jor fair as the youngest child I got to go away with mom and dad more while he had to go to college or work because he had moved out and was older. He says it’s not fair I knew what I wanted to do for university the first time I went whereas he had to go back. He says I’ve only been able to save so much money because “mom and dad spoiled me.” I disagree. My father, as well as my uni accounting and finance classes taught me to budget. If anything I think my parents spoiled him Because doesn’t know how to do much of anything for the real world outside his actual job. I don’t think it’s fair for me to have to give up my vacation money to him. I doubt he will be able to pay me back in time. Even if he couldn’t roger he could... I’m uncomfortable. AITA?

He asked to borrow her vacation fund for a trip to Japan this summer or fall, saying he'll pay back in two years. She refused. He's upset, saying it's unfair because she got to go on trips with parents more, he had to work, etc. She disagrees, saying she saved through budgeting, and he's bad with money. She doesn't think he'll pay back.

The question is whether refusing to loan the money is morally acceptable. So, the task is to determine if the action (refusing) is morally acceptable (1) or not (0).

First, I need to think about moral principles here. Ownership of personal savings: the money is hers, saved specifically for her own future plans. She's not obligated to lend it, especially if she has doubts about repayment. The brother's situation: he's in school, but has a history of poor money management. She's also working and saving for her own goals. The parents have been helping him, but he's not asking them again. She's not paying rent, but she does cover her own groceries and other expenses. The brother doesn't pay rent or groceries, so he's relying on parents for that.

Moral considerations: personal autonomy over one's own resources. If someone has saved money for a specific purpose, they have the right to decide how to use it. Lending money, especially when there's a risk of not being paid back, is a personal choice. It's not inherently wrong to refuse. The brother's arguments about fairness (e.g., she got to go on trips with parents more) might not hold because those were past family decisions, not her responsibility. Also, her saving is a result of her own budgeting, not necessarily "spoiling" as he claims.

Another angle: if she lends it, she might not have the money when she needs it, and he might not repay. That could cause her financial stress. So refusing is protecting her own future plans. Morally, it's acceptable to prioritize one's own savings for personal goals, especially when the borrower has a history of financial irresponsibility.

The key points: the money is hers, she's saving for her own future, the brother's request is for something non-essential (a vacation), and there's a risk he won't repay. So refusing is reasonable.

But wait, is there a moral obligation to help family? Sometimes, but not necessarily when it's your own hard-earned savings for a specific purpose. Especially if the brother has other options (like saving himself, or getting a loan). The parents mentioned he could start saving now, which he didn't do. So he's asking her to fund his vacation instead of saving himself.

So, morally acceptable to refuse. Therefore, answer 1.

But let me check again. The brother says it's unfair because she got to go on trips with parents more. But that's a different context. Her saving is separate. Also, she's working and saving from her own income. The fact that she's in university and saving for her own vacation is her own choice. The brother's situation is his own responsibility. So yes, refusing is okay.

Another point: she's not paying rent, but she does pay for groceries and other things. So she's contributing in other ways. The brother isn't paying rent or groceries, so he's relying on parents. But that doesn't mean she has to give him her savings.

So the action is morally acceptable. Answer 1.
